source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Embodied Cognition (extended mind section)
finding: Adams and Aizawa say the extended-mind argument slides from 'coupled to' a process to 'part of' it (coupling-constitution fallacy). Rupert says Otto's notebook use and Inga's memory differ too much to be one natural kind, and that tools are used by a cognitive system, not parts of it. Clark replies with functional parity and brain 'impartiality'.
numbers: No quantitative results; the arguments rest on thought experiments (Otto and Inga, Wilson's wide computationalism).
limits: Page read only to character 100000 of 114500. The dispute is philosophical, so no experiment decides it.
agent_relevance: The 'tool use vs constituent' dispute is not settled by data. For our agent, count notes as part of the thinking loop by what they measurably do (retrieval, checks), not by the label.

source: Gong and Yang (2024) Google effects on memory: a meta-analytical review of the media effects of intensive Internet search behavior (Frontiers in Public Health)
finding: Meta-analysis of 'Google effect' studies reports a moderate, significant pooled effect, but with very wide spread (d from -0.85 to 4.38). Only some sub-types had confidence intervals that excluded zero.
numbers: 22 articles, 35 independent comparisons, 30,889 participants (ages 12-89), studies 2011-2021. Subgroups: cognitive load d=0.73 [0.22,1.24]; behavioural phenotype 0.39 [0.16,0.61]; cognitive self-esteem 0.91 [0.23,1.59]; cognitive measurement 0.56 [-0.15,1.28]; psychophysiology 1.01 [-0.12,2.13]. Only region (Europe vs North America) explained heterogeneity (Q=6.20, 13.18%); publication year, sample size, sex did not.
limits: Low rigour: published studies only, mixed outcome types lumped together, funnel plot judged by eye, a d of 4.38 is implausible. The pooled d itself was not stated in the text I read. Many included studies do not test memory offloading directly.
agent_relevance: Do not lean on 'search weakens memory' as a firm effect. Direction is moderately supported, size is uncertain.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015 (includes Sparrow et al. 2011)
finding: Large replication project of 21 Science/Nature studies included the Sparrow et al. 'Google Stroop' experiment. It did not replicate despite adequate power, as described in the later paper I did read (b04).
numbers: Sparrow-specific figures not seen. Page fetch returned only a truncated reference list.
limits: Not opened (paywall, truncated). The original author later noted design differences (cognitive-load manipulation, materials not shared with the replicators).
agent_relevance: Priming of internet concepts by missing knowledge is not a safe foundation for design.

source: Replication of the 'Google Stroop effect' (PeerJ 2020; Psychologische Hochschule Berlin): No conclusive evidence that difficult general knowledge questions cause a Google Stroop effect
finding: Closer replication of Sparrow et al. Exp 1 with the original author's critiques addressed. Hard questions did not slow color-naming of computer words. Bayes factor favoured the null about 5 to 1.
numbers: N=117 tested, N=89 in final sequential Bayes analysis. Easy-question accuracy 97%, hard 60% (original: 98% vs 47%). Easy block RT: general 830 ms, computer 901 ms. Hard block RT: general 825 ms, computer 821 ms. BF01=5.07; BF01 about 16 against the exact original pattern.
limits: Students plus friends and family; undergraduate project; BF of 5 is only moderate evidence. Does not test the where-vs-what recall half of Sparrow's paper.
agent_relevance: The automatic-search-priming half of the famous 'Google effect' has two failed replications (Camerer 2018 and this one). Weak support for designing around it.
quote: Our results revealed no conclusive evidence in favor of the notion that the concept of the Internet

source: Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011) Google effects on memory: cognitive consequences of having information at our fingertips
finding: Four experiments: people who expect future access to information recall it less and recall where to find it better; hard trivia questions prime internet words.
numbers: Original Exp 1 hard-question accuracy 47% vs easy 98% (as quoted in b04). Other numbers not seen this session.
limits: Not opened. I did not read a large replication of the memory half (Exp 2-4).
agent_relevance: Foundational claim that an external store changes what is encoded. For our agent, that applies only if the note store changes what the agent writes down.

source: Grinschgl, Papenmeier and Meyerhoff (2021) Consequences of cognitive offloading: boosting performance but diminishing memory (QJEP)
finding: Pattern Copy Task: more offloading gave faster, equally accurate task performance but worse memory for the offloaded items in a surprise test. Knowing a memory test was coming largely removed the cost, even when offloading was forced.
numbers: Three experiments, N=172 each. Exp 1: more-offloading group remembered identity worse, t(170)=-2.76, p=.006, eta2=.04; identity-location bindings t(170)=-2.63, p=.009. Trials faster t(170)=-3.31, p=.001, with no accuracy loss (t=-0.37). Exp 3: forced/uninformed group worse than all others, t(84)>=4.17, eta2>=.18; interaction F(1,168)=6.89, p=.009.
limits: Lab task with picture patterns; online sample; surprise memory test; small to medium effects.
agent_relevance: Offloading helps now and costs later unless the learner intends to retain. An agent that writes notes still needs an explicit instruction about what to carry forward.

source: Hu, Luo and Fleming (2019) A role for metamemory in cognitive offloading (Cognition)
finding: People chose to save the harder word pairs and used the saved copy to boost recall. Confidence in unaided memory predicted whether they asked for help. A model in which belief in the hint's benefit is negatively coupled to memory confidence fitted the data.
numbers: Four experiments (Exp 2a N=27 lab; Exp 2b N=40 online replication). Criterion for asking for help was more liberal for easy than difficult trials, mean difference 0.186, 95% CI [0.070, 0.295].
limits: Word-pair task; small samples; saving is an instructed manipulation, not natural notes.
agent_relevance: Offloading is driven by metacognitive confidence, not true ability. Trigger note lookup on a measured low-confidence signal (matches G1), not on a schedule.

source: Confidence guides spontaneous cognitive offloading (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 2019)
finding: With no instructions on how to use reminders, people still set reminders more often when less confident. Uninstructed people set fewer reminders than instructed people. Offloading improved performance in both groups.
numbers: 435 recruited (MTurk), 363 analysed; powered to detect d=0.2.
limits: Delayed-intention computer task; MTurk sample; reminders are a simple tool.
agent_relevance: Without being told, agents under-use external memory. Hard-wire the note step into the loop rather than hoping the model chooses it.

source: Offloading items from memory: individual differences in cognitive offloading in a short-term memory task (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 2020; registered replication of Risko and Dunn 2015)
finding: Registered report replicating and extending Risko and Dunn (2015). Offloading beat internal memory, most at higher loads. The new prediction (low working-memory-capacity people offload more or gain more) failed.
numbers: N=114 final (130 recruited, 16 excluded), two sites; set sizes 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 letters.
limits: Undergraduates only. Author names not recorded.
agent_relevance: Benefit grows with load, so notes matter most on long tasks. Do not assume weaker models benefit more.

source: Does taking multiple photos lead to a photo-taking-impairment effect? (Psychonomic Bulletin and Review, 2022)
finding: Photographing paintings reduced memory for them (photo-taking impairment, first shown by Henkel 2014). It persists with five photos and with non-selective photographing.
numbers: Exp 1 N=60 within subjects: Observe vs 5-Photo d=0.35 [0.09,0.61], p=.009; Observe vs 1-Photo d=0.16 ns; linear trend F(1,59)=7.24, p=.009. Exps 2 and 3 replicated the pattern in between-subjects designs.
limits: Small effect; undergraduates; paintings in lab; single-photo effect was not significant in Exp 1.
agent_relevance: Recording something can stand in for holding it. If the scratch pad carries the detail, expect later steps to depend on the pad.

source: Nijssen et al. (2018) Has your smartphone replaced your brain? Construction and validation of the Extended Mind Questionnaire (PLOS ONE)
finding: Built and validated a 12-item scale measuring how far people offload cognitive and social functions to digital devices. Reliable in young adults and teenagers.
numbers: Study 1 n=63; Study 2 teenagers n=947 (ages 12-18).
limits: Self-report; measures reliance, not whether the mind is truly extended.
agent_relevance: Individual differences in tool reliance exist in people. For agents, reliance is a setting we control.

source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) The Extended Mind; Clark (2008) Supersizing the Mind; Wilson (2004)
finding: Parity principle: if a process in the world works like one we would call cognitive in the head, it is cognitive. Otto's notebook counts as memory if it is reliably available, automatically trusted, easily accessed and was endorsed when stored.
numbers: None; thought experiment.
limits: Not opened. The four conditions are from the general literature, not read this session.
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist for when a note store should count as memory: always reachable, trusted without re-checking, cheap to access, written by the agent earlier.

source: Adams and Aizawa (2001, 2008) The Bounds of Cognition; Rupert (2004) Challenges to the hypothesis of extended cognition
finding: Critics: intrinsic (non-derived) content marks the cognitive; external notes carry only derived content; tools are embedded, not constituent.
numbers: None.
limits: Known only through the SEP summary I read (b01); originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Even critics accept that notes help (embedding); the dispute does not change engineering.

source: Packer et al. (2023) MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
finding: Giving a fixed-context LLM a tiered external memory it reads and writes by tool calls greatly raises recall of earlier chat sessions.
numbers: Deep memory retrieval accuracy: GPT-3.5 Turbo 38.7% to 66.9% with MemGPT; GPT-4 32.1% to 92.5%; GPT-4 Turbo 35.3% to 93.4%.
limits: Own benchmark; baselines are fixed-context truncation, not RAG with a good index; one dataset (multi-session chat).
agent_relevance: Strong direct evidence that a model-managed external memory lifts memory-bound tasks. Much of the gain compensates for truncation.

source: Klett and Ahle (2024) Extended Mind Transformers
finding: Model attends to retrieved key-value memories using its own attention, with no fine-tuning. Retrieval in most decoder layers matters.
numbers: Retrieval accuracy at 2k/4k/8k/16k: Extended Mind Llama2-7b 38.59/37.95/36.00/33.54%; base Chat Llama2 42.74/41.96/33.50/17.68%. Extended Mind 70b+RAG 59.34/53.13/53.00/50.00% vs GPT-4 52.28/50.00/46.00/43.29%. Claimed gain 6% over GPT-4 on average.
limits: At short input the base model is better; gain appears only at long lengths. Authors' own counterfactual benchmark.
agent_relevance: External memory helps only when the task exceeds context; at short length it can cost accuracy.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Written self-reflections kept in an episodic buffer improve agents across trials. Ablation: reflection adds beyond raw episodic memory of the last trajectory.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1. On 100 HotPotQA questions self-reflection gave 8% absolute gain over episodic memory alone. Gains over baselines: 22% AlfWorld, 20% HotPotQA, 11% HumanEval.
limits: 100-question HotPotQA test; possible HumanEval contamination; reflection uses real test feedback.
agent_relevance: Notes help most when they distil a failure grounded in real output (matches G2). Raw replay helps less.
quote: reflection improves learning by an 8% absolute boost over the episodic memory learning advantage

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
finding: Removing memory, reflection and planning from simulated agents reduced believability rated by 100 human evaluators.
numbers: TrueSkill believability: full 29.89; no reflection 26.88; no reflection or planning 25.64; human crowdworker 22.95; no memory, planning or reflection 21.21.
limits: Rated on interview answers, not task success; one sandbox world.
agent_relevance: Each memory layer adds value; reflection (notes about notes) adds value after raw memory.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with LLMs
finding: A growing library of executable skills stored outside the model is a core part of lifelong learning in Minecraft.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distance, tech milestones up to 15.3x faster than prior SOTA. Ablations: random curriculum -93% items; no self-verification -73%; no skill library plateaus in later stages.
limits: Single environment; needs GPT-4 (GPT-3.5 code generation clearly worse); skills are code and can be checked.
agent_relevance: The store works because entries are verified code, not opinion. Store only what passed a check.

source: Maharana et al. (2024) LoCoMo: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents
finding: Long-context models and RAG help but remain far below humans on very long conversations, worst on time reasoning and adversarial questions.
numbers: Best model gpt-4-turbo overall 32.4 vs human 87.9. RAG improves 22-66% but is still 56% below human; temporal reasoning 73% below. Adversarial questions: gpt-3.5-turbo-16k 2.1%, Llama-2-Chat 22.1%, gpt-4-turbo 4K 70.2%. gpt-3.5-16k lost 3.0% precision and 8.7% recall vs its 4K version on event summaries.
limits: Conversations were machine-generated then edited by annotators (about 15% of turns edited).
agent_relevance: A bigger window is not a better notebook. Retrieval structure and time stamps matter.

source: Wu et al. (2024) LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory
finding: Commercial assistants and long-context models drop sharply on sustained-interaction memory. Storage granularity, key expansion and timestamps move accuracy.
numbers: 500 questions; long-context LLMs show 30-60% drop on the S set (about 115k tokens); commercial systems 30-70% accuracy in a simpler setting. Key expansion with extracted facts: +9.4% recall@k and +5.4% QA accuracy. Time-aware indexing: +6.8 to 11.3% temporal recall. Round-level storage beats session-level.
limits: Benchmark built by the authors; a limited set of LLMs tested.
agent_relevance: Direct design evidence: store by turn, index with extracted facts, time-stamp. Perfect recall still does not guarantee correct use.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Models use information at the start and end of context best and lose it in the middle. Extra retrieved documents beyond about 20 add little.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA can drop by more than 20% depending on position; at 20 and 30 documents it can fall below closed-book. More than 20 retrieved documents adds only about 1.5% (GPT-3.5-Turbo).
limits: 2023-era models; newer models improved; QA with distractors.
agent_relevance: Putting everything in the prompt is not a good external memory. Place key notes first or last and keep the set small.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
finding: Writing essays with an LLM showed weaker EEG connectivity, lower ownership and worse recall of one's own essay than writing with search or alone.
numbers: 54 participants in 3 groups; 18 completed session 4. Failed to quote own essay: LLM 83.3% (15/18) vs 11.1% (2/18) in each of Search and Brain-only. Connectivity scaled down with external support.
limits: Small N, preprint under review, EEG claims exploratory.
agent_relevance: Human-side warning that strong help can reduce engagement. Not about agent behaviour.

source: Storm and Stone (2015) Saving-enhanced memory: the benefits of saving on the learning and remembering of new information
finding: Saving a file frees resources so that new material is learned better. Europe PMC lists later work on partial saving and working memory capacity (2024-2025); not read.
numbers: Not read; numbers not recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Notes can free capacity for the next step. Supports a scratch pad for intermediate results.

source: Fisher, Goddu and Keil (2015) Searching for explanations: how the Internet inflates estimates of internal knowledge
finding: After searching online, people rate their own knowledge higher, even for unrelated questions.
numbers: Not read; numbers not recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Source-confusion risk: an agent reading its own notes may overrate unaided competence. Keep sources labelled.

source: Risko and Gilbert (2016) Cognitive offloading (Trends in Cognitive Sciences)
finding: Framework paper that several of the papers I read use: offloading is chosen by a cost-benefit estimate shaped by metacognition.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened; known through citations in b06-b08.
agent_relevance: Offloading is a decision driven by confidence, not capacity.

source: Synthesis across b01-b24: what discriminates extended-mind from embedded-use
finding: No experiment I read discriminates the two views. The findings (offloading is guided by confidence, costs later memory unless learning is intended, helps most at high load) are predicted by both.
numbers: Derived from earlier lines.
limits: Judgment of the research agent, not a source finding.
agent_relevance: Build to the shared prediction: note use that is automatic, reliable, grounded in checked output, and triggered by a measured signal.
